nations: Georgia Yazoo land purchasers; Creek and Cherokee lands in Georgia [unverified: V1 found no Creek or Cherokee reference in the opinion text read; tribes are not named there]
holding_summary: Held that a Georgia land grant was a contract the legislature could not rescind (Contracts Clause). Marshall's opinion also described Georgia's title as subject to an Indian right of occupancy, an early step toward the discovery doctrine [Indian-title dicta from-memory].

nations: Illinois and Piankeshaw peoples (private deeds c. 1773-1775)
holding_summary: Courts of the United States will not recognize land titles obtained directly from tribes by private persons. Discovery gave the European sovereign, and the U.S. as successor, ultimate title and the exclusive power to extinguish a tribal right of occupancy.

treaty_at_issue: Treaty of Hopewell (1785) and later Cherokee treaties
holding_summary: The Cherokee Nation is not a 'foreign state' for Article III original jurisdiction, so the Court could not hear its suit against Georgia; injunction denied. Marshall characterized tribes as 'domestic dependent nations' in a guardian-ward relationship.

Georgia's law requiring non-Indians to obtain a state license to reside in Cherokee territory was void; the Cherokee Nation is a distinct political community whose relations are governed exclusively by the federal government. Georgia and President Jackson did not enforce the judgment [enforcement history from-memory].
An 1868 act of Congress extending liquor and tobacco taxes to Cherokee territory overrode the treaty's exemption: a later act of Congress can supersede an earlier treaty.

full_citation: United States ex rel. Standing Bear v. Crook, 25 F. Cas. 695 (C.C.D. Neb. 1879) (No. 14,891)
court: U.S. Circuit Court, D. Neb. (Judge Dundy)
treaty_at_issue: Ponca treaties of 1858 and 1865; 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty mistakenly assigned Ponca land to the Sioux
holding_summary: An Indian is a 'person' entitled to petition for habeas corpus, and no treaty or statute authorized forcibly removing peaceable Ponca to Indian Territory against their will; the relators were discharged.

treaty_at_issue: Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 and 1877 Agreement
holding_summary: A federal territorial court lacked jurisdiction to try one Indian for killing another on the Great Sioux Reservation; the statutory exception for intra-Indian crimes was not repealed by the 1868 treaty or 1877 agreement. Congress responded with the Major Crimes Act (1885).

nations: Individual born into a tribe (John Elk)
holding_summary: A man born into a recognized tribe who left it and lived among non-Indians, without naturalization or federal recognition as a citizen, was not a Fourteenth Amendment citizen. Citizenship was later conferred by statute (1924).

treaty_at_issue: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830) and later Choctaw treaties [Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830) verified; "and later Choctaw treaties" remains from-memory]
holding_summary: Treated the Senate's 1859 arbitration award as the closest approximation of justice and held the Choctaw entitled to further sums for unpaid annuities and land lost in the Arkansas boundary survey. Often cited for reading treaties as the Indians understood them [pin cite from-memory].

Upheld the Major Crimes Act as applied to an Indian-on-Indian murder on a reservation within a state, reasoning that Congress has authority to govern tribes because they are dependent wards and states cannot.

The Fifth Amendment grand-jury requirement does not bind the Cherokee Nation's own laws, because tribal self-government predates the Constitution and is not a delegation of federal power. Led indirectly to the Indian Civil Rights Act (1968).

Held Wyoming's admission to the Union ended the Bannock treaty right to hunt on unoccupied federal land, so a tribal member could be prosecuted under state game law. Later undermined by Mille Lacs (1999) and effectively rejected in Herrera (2019).

A treaty can convey alienable fee title to an individual tribal member without a patent; a treaty 'must therefore be construed not according to the technical meaning of its words to learned lawyers' [partial quote verified].

Congress has plenary power over tribal relations; a treaty requirement of three-fourths adult-male consent did not bar Congress from opening the Kiowa-Comanche-Apache reservation to allotment and sale by statute. The Court called the matter political and non-justiciable.

treaty_at_issue: Treaty of 1855 with the Yakama (12 Stat. 951)
holding_summary: The treaty right to fish at usual and accustomed places was a right reserved by the Yakama from land they ceded, not a grant to them; it burdened the ceded land against the United States' grantees and the state, and statehood did not extinguish it.

nations: Gros Ventre (A'aninin) and Assiniboine (Nakoda), Fort Belknap
holding_summary: The 1888 agreement creating Fort Belknap impliedly reserved enough Milk River water for the reservation's purposes; Montana's statehood did not defeat that reserved right (the 'Winters doctrine').

Oklahoma's tax on allottees' oil and gas royalty interests violated the agreement's tax exemption; 'Doubtful expressions are to be resolved in favor of the weak and defenseless people who are the wards of the nation' [quote verified].
The government's appropriation of Creek tribal land through disposals under the 1891 Act was a taking requiring compensation valued as of the taking plus 5 percent interest.

Where a treaty recognized the Shoshone's right to the reservation, later government placement of Arapaho there was a compensable taking; damages measured from the 1878 unlawful occupation plus added compensation such as interest.

short_name: United States v. Santa Fe Pacific R. Co.
holding_summary: Walapai request for and acceptance of the 1883 reservation relinquished their claims to outside lands. Frequently cited for the principle that extinguishment of aboriginal title is for Congress ('by treaty, by the sword, by purchase...').

The government owes tribes a strict fiduciary duty; the Court of Claims had to decide whether officials knew tribal leaders were defrauding members when payments were made. Foundational for the modern trust doctrine.
Washington may apply nonfee conservation rules to treaty fishing but cannot charge Yakama fishers license fees that burden the treaty right.

short_name: Northwestern Bands of Shoshone Indians v. United States
holding_summary: The 1863 treaty did not recognize Indian title to the lands claimed, so the claim did not arise under the treaty and was not recoverable under the 1929 jurisdictional act. Illustrates the recognized-title / aboriginal-title divide.
Unrecognized aboriginal occupancy is not property protected by the Fifth Amendment; Congress may extinguish it without compensation. Douglas, joined by Warren and Frankfurter, dissented.

full_citation: Seneca Nation of Indians v. Brucker, 262 F.2d 27 (D.C. Cir. 1958) (per curiam) [cert. history unverified]
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, D.C. Cir.
holding_summary: Courts declined to block taking of about 10,000 acres of the Allegany Reservation for Kinzua Dam, treating Congress's later authorization as controlling over the 1794 treaty. Congress later paid compensation and funded relocation [Pub. L. 89-801 from-memory].

A state court could not hear a non-Indian trader's collection suit against Navajo residents over an on-reservation transaction, because that would infringe the Navajos' right to make their own laws and be ruled by them.

short_name: Federal Power Commission v. Tuscarora Indian Nation
treaty_at_issue: none for the fee lands at issue (purchased in fee)
holding_summary: Tuscarora lands owned in fee simple are not a 'reservation' under the Federal Power Act, so a licensee may condemn them for a power project (Niagara) on paying compensation; 25 U.S.C. 177 did not bar the taking. Black, Warren and Douglas dissented.

short_name: Seymour v. Superintendent of Washington State Penitentiary
nations: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation
holding_summary: The Colville Reservation still existed despite opening part of it to non-Indian settlement; a burglary on non-Indian land within the borders was in 'Indian country' and outside Washington's criminal jurisdiction. First of the modern diminishment cases.

nations: Colorado River Indian Tribes, Fort Mojave, Chemehuevi, Quechan, Cocopah [from-memory]
holding_summary: Allocated Lower Colorado River water under the Boulder Canyon Project Act. Also confirmed reserved water rights for the Colorado River reservations, quantified by 'practicably irrigable acreage' [confirmed from the Justia syllabus by V1; Part V of the opinion text was truncated and not read].

short_name: Menominee Tribe of Indians v. United States
holding_summary: The 1854 treaty phrase 'to be held as Indian lands are held' included hunting and fishing rights, and the Menominee Termination Act of 1954 (read with Public Law 280) did not extinguish them; courts do not lightly infer abrogation.

short_name: Puyallup Tribe v. Department of Game (Puyallup I)
holding_summary: Washington may regulate off-reservation treaty fishing for conservation if the rules are nondiscriminatory and meet appropriate standards. Sets up the Boldt litigation.

court: U.S. District Court, D. Or. (Judge Belloni)
nations: Yakama, Warm Springs, Umatilla, Nez Perce (Columbia River tribes)
treaty_at_issue: 1855 treaties of the Columbia Plateau tribes [from-memory; the Wikipedia page V1 read does not mention the 1855 treaties]
holding_summary: Recognized tribal treaty fishing rights on the Columbia River with limits on state regulation and a 'fair and equitable share'; consolidated with United States v. Oregon.

The Act of June 17, 1892, which opened the Klamath River Reservation to settlement, did not terminate it; allotment provisions were consistent with continued reservation status absent clear congressional intent.

short_name: McClanahan v. Arizona State Tax Commission
holding_summary: Arizona could not tax the income of a Navajo living and earning on the reservation: treaty and statutes reserve that area to the federal government and the tribe. Revived tribal sovereignty as a backdrop against which federal statutes are read.

nations: Employees of the Bureau of Indian Affairs (not a specific nation)
holding_summary: The BIA's Indian hiring preference survived the 1972 anti-discrimination law and does not violate Fifth Amendment due process, because it is a political, not racial, classification tied to Indian self-government.

short_name: Oneida Indian Nation v. County of Oneida (Oneida I)
treaty_at_issue: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784); Treaty of Canandaigua (1794); claim based on 1795 state conveyance
holding_summary: The Oneidas' claim to possessory rights under the Nonintercourse Act arises under federal law, supporting federal-question jurisdiction; Indian title is governed by federal law and can be extinguished only with federal consent.

court: U.S. District Court, W.D. Wash. (Judge Boldt)
nations: Stevens treaty tribes of western Washington (e.g., Puyallup, Nisqually, Lummi, Suquamish, Tulalip)
treaty_at_issue: Treaties of Medicine Creek, Point Elliott, Point No Point, Neah Bay, Olympia (1854-55)
holding_summary: Read the treaty phrase 'in common with' to give treaty tribes up to half of the harvestable fish at usual and accustomed places; state regulation allowed only as necessary for conservation.
The 1891 Act terminated the Lake Traverse Reservation, so South Dakota had jurisdiction over tribal members' conduct on non-Indian unallotted lands within the 1867 boundaries. Douglas dissented.

short_name: Joint Tribal Council of the Passamaquoddy Tribe v. Morton
holding_summary: The Nonintercourse Act protects any tribe, including one not federally recognized, and creates a federal trust relationship Maine could not end; this opened the way to the Maine land claims and the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act (1980).
Public Law 280's civil grant did not authorize states to tax reservation Indians; PL 280 conferred adjudicatory, not general regulatory, civil authority.

treaty_at_issue: Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 | acts of 1904, 1907, 1910
holding_summary: Congress's 1904, 1907 and 1910 acts opening Rosebud lands to settlement showed clear intent to shrink the reservation, despite the absence of treaty-required tribal consent.

Tribal courts have no inherent criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians absent congressional authorization, on an 'implicit divestiture' theory. Partly reversed in effect by VAWA 2013/2022. Marshall and Burger dissented.

Tribal sovereign immunity bars federal civil suits to enforce the Indian Civil Rights Act against the tribe or its officers; habeas under 25 U.S.C. 1303 is the only federal remedy. Tribes decide membership.
A tribe prosecuting its own members acts as an independent sovereign, so Double Jeopardy does not bar a later federal prosecution; tribal criminal power is inherent, not delegated.

short_name: Mashpee Tribe v. New Seabury Corp.
holding_summary: Upheld a jury finding that the Mashpee were a 'tribe' in 1834 and 1843 but not in 1790 or at suit, defeating a Nonintercourse Act land claim. The Tribe won federal acknowledgment in 2007.

short_name: Washington v. Washington State Commercial Passenger Fishing Vessel Ass'n
nations: Stevens treaty tribes of western Washington
holding_summary: Affirmed Boldt: treaty fishing 'in common with' citizens entitles tribes to a fair share (up to 50 percent) of each harvestable run, and state law cannot prevent compliance with the federal decree.

short_name: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians
nations: Great Sioux Nation (Oceti Sakowin) | Lakota, Dakota, Nakota
treaty_at_issue: Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 (15 Stat. 635); Act of Feb. 28, 1877
holding_summary: The 1877 Act took Black Hills land that the 1868 treaty reserved, so the government owed just compensation plus interest; Congress could waive res judicata. Remedy was money only; the Sioux have declined payment and continue to seek land return.

short_name: White Mountain Apache Tribe v. Bracker
holding_summary: State motor-carrier and fuel taxes on a non-Indian logging contractor operating solely on the reservation were preempted by pervasive federal regulation of tribal timber; case-specific interest-balancing for preemption.

Title to the Big Horn riverbed passed to Montana at statehood. Tribes lack inherent civil authority over non-members on non-Indian fee land, subject to two exceptions (consensual relationships; conduct threatening the tribe's political integrity, economic security, health or welfare): the 'Montana rule'.
The Tribe may impose a severance tax on non-Indian lessees' oil and gas production on the reservation as an inherent attribute of sovereignty tied to the power to exclude.

short_name: New Mexico v. Mescalero Apache Tribe
holding_summary: New Mexico cannot apply its hunting and fishing laws to non-members on the reservation; federal law preempts concurrent state regulation and the state showed no sufficient interest.

treaty_at_issue: Act of 1889 (reservation); Cheyenne River Act of 1908
holding_summary: The 1908 Act opened reservation land to non-Indian homesteaders without diminishing the reservation; a clear congressional intent to diminish is required, judged by statutory text, contemporaneous history, and (secondarily) later events. Sets the three-part Solem framework.

nations: Blackfeet Nation (Siksika/Pikuni) | Blackfeet Tribe of Montana
holding_summary: Montana could not tax the Tribe's oil and gas royalty income under 1938 Indian Mineral Leasing Act leases because Congress never clearly consented; statutes are liberally construed for Indians.

short_name: Oneida County v. Oneida Indian Nation (Oneida II)
treaty_at_issue: Nonintercourse Act of 1793; 1795 conveyance to New York
holding_summary: Tribes may sue under federal common law to enforce possessory rights in land conveyed in violation of the Nonintercourse Act, rejecting limitations, abatement, ratification and political-question defenses. Opened modern eastern land claims.

short_name: Oregon Dept. of Fish & Wildlife v. Klamath Indian Tribe
treaty_at_issue: Treaty of 1864 with the Klamath and Modoc; Agreement of 1901
holding_summary: The 1901 cession agreement ended the Tribe's exclusive off-reservation hunting and fishing privileges on ceded lands, leaving them open to state regulation. Marshall and Brennan dissented.

treaty_at_issue: none discussed in opinion (Indian Claims Commission Act proceedings); Treaty of Ruby Valley (1863) is background [needs source]
holding_summary: Under the Indian Claims Commission Act, 'payment' of a tribal award occurred when funds were deposited in a Treasury trust account, which the Court held extinguished Western Shoshone aboriginal title claims. Western Shoshone dispute that their title was extinguished and the dispute continues.

short_name: California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians
holding_summary: California could not enforce its bingo and card-room laws on reservations: Public Law 280 does not give states regulatory power and state interests did not outweigh federal and tribal interests. Led to IGRA (1988).

The original escheat provision of the Indian Land Consolidation Act (1983), abolishing descent and devise of tiny fractional interests without compensation, was an unconstitutional taking. Illustrates allotment-era fractionation.

short_name: Lyng v. Northwest Indian Cemetery Protective Ass'n
holding_summary: The Free Exercise Clause does not bar the government from building a road or allowing logging on federal land (Chimney Rock, Six Rivers National Forest) even if it severely burdens Native religious practice; AIRFA creates no judicially enforceable rights.

short_name: Brendale v. Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Indian Nation
holding_summary: Fractured decision: the Tribe may zone non-Indian fee land in the 'closed' area of the reservation but not in the 'open' area. Applies Montana's logic to checkerboard land.

nations: Native American Church members (Klamath) [unverified: V1 did not find '(Klamath)' in the opinion text read]
holding_summary: The Free Exercise Clause does not exempt people from neutral laws of general applicability, so Oregon could criminalize sacramental peyote use and deny unemployment benefits. Prompted RFRA (1993) and AIRFA amendments (1994).

nations: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
holding_summary: Congress diminished the Uintah Valley Reservation when it opened unallotted lands to settlement, so Myton was not Indian country and Utah had jurisdiction. Blackmun and Souter dissented.

short_name: Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida
holding_summary: Congress cannot use the Indian Commerce Clause to abrogate state sovereign immunity under the Eleventh Amendment; the IGRA suit mechanism against states was invalid.

Tribal courts lack jurisdiction over a negligence suit between non-members arising on a state-maintained highway right-of-way across the reservation; the right-of-way was treated as non-Indian land under Montana.

short_name: Alaska v. Native Village of Venetie Tribal Government
holding_summary: ANCSA lands conveyed to a village corporation are not 'Indian country' because they lack a federal set-aside and federal superintendence, so the tribe could not tax non-members. Largely removed Alaska from the Indian-country framework.

short_name: Kiowa Tribe of Oklahoma v. Manufacturing Technologies, Inc.
holding_summary: Tribes are immune from contract suits, whether commercial or governmental and on or off the reservation, absent congressional abrogation or tribal waiver; the Court left any reform to Congress.

short_name: South Dakota v. Yankton Sioux Tribe
holding_summary: The 1894 Act ratifying the sale of unallotted surplus lands diminished the reservation; ceded lands are no longer Indian country. Unanimous.

short_name: Minnesota v. Mille Lacs Band of Chippewa Indians
nations: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) and other Chippewa bands
holding_summary: The 1837 treaty's usufructuary hunting, fishing and gathering rights survived: the 1850 removal order was invalid, the 1855 treaty did not abrogate them, and statehood did not extinguish them. 5-4.

treaty_at_issue: Executive order of 1873 and agreement/act of 1889-1891
holding_summary: The United States holds title in trust for the Tribe to the submerged lands under parts of Lake Coeur d'Alene and the St. Joe River; the tribe's historic dependence on the lake supported a purposeful reservation. Rehnquist dissented.

Tribal courts lacked jurisdiction over tort and civil-rights claims against state game wardens who executed a search warrant at a tribal member's reservation home for an off-reservation offense; extends Montana to tribal-member land.

short_name: United States v. Navajo Nation (Navajo I)
holding_summary: The Indian Mineral Leasing Act and regulations impose no enforceable fiduciary duty supporting money damages for the Secretary's approval of a coal-lease royalty; the general trust relationship alone is not enough. Souter dissented.

nations: Spirit Lake Tribe; Lara was a Turtle Mountain Band member
holding_summary: Congress may relax restrictions on tribes' inherent authority to prosecute non-member Indians (the 1991 'Duro fix'), so tribal and federal prosecutions are by separate sovereigns.

short_name: Cayuga Indian Nation of New York v. Pataki
treaty_at_issue: Conveyances of 1795 and 1807 (64,015 acres); Treaty of Canandaigua (1794) [Canandaigua: unverified, not found on the Wikipedia page V1 read; the 1795/1807 conveyances and 64,015 acres are confirmed there]
holding_summary: Laches bars possessory land claims in the nature of ejectment; vacated a roughly $247.9 million judgment, applying Sherrill broadly. Hall dissented.

short_name: City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation of New York
nations: Oneida Indian Nation of New York (Haudenosaunee)
treaty_at_issue: Treaty of Fort Schuyler (1788); Treaty of Canandaigua (1794)
holding_summary: The Oneida could not revive tribal sovereignty over parcels repurchased on the open market after about two centuries of state and local control; laches, acquiescence and impossibility bar that relief. The route is trust acquisition (25 U.S.C. 5108, then 465).

short_name: Navajo Nation v. U.S. Forest Service
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, 9th Cir. (en banc)
nations: Navajo Nation, Hopi Tribe, Havasupai and other tribes of the San Francisco Peaks [from-memory]
holding_summary: Using reclaimed wastewater for snowmaking on the San Francisco Peaks was not a 'substantial burden' under RFRA because the statute reaches only coercion or choice between religious practice and a benefit. Precedent later applied to Oak Flat.

short_name: Plains Commerce Bank v. Long Family Land & Cattle Co.
holding_summary: A tribal court lacked jurisdiction over a non-member bank's sale of non-Indian fee land within the reservation; Montana's exceptions did not reach it. 5-4.

'Now under Federal jurisdiction' in the Indian Reorganization Act means under federal jurisdiction in 1934, so the Secretary could not take land into trust for a tribe not then under federal jurisdiction. Interior later adopted a two-part test; Congress has not enacted a legislative fix [status as of 2026 unverified].

short_name: Cobell v. Salazar (individual Indian trust litigation)
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, D.C. Cir.
nations: Individual Indian trust beneficiaries (class; lead plaintiff Elouise Cobell, Blackfeet)
holding_summary: Vacated a $455.6 million award; the class action begun in 1996 ended in a $3.4 billion settlement funded by the Claims Resolution Act of 2010, approved Aug. 4, 2011 and final Nov. 24, 2012, including a $1.9 billion Land Consolidation Fund.

short_name: United States v. Jicarilla Apache Nation
holding_summary: The fiduciary exception to attorney-client privilege does not apply to the general trust relationship between the United States and tribes, which is defined by statute and exercised in the government's sovereign capacity.

Assuming the father was an ICWA 'parent', he could not invoke ICWA's heightened protections against termination of his rights because he never had custody and no alternative placement was sought; ICWA's adoptive-placement preferences also did not apply.

short_name: Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian Community
treaty_at_issue: Treaty of 1836 (land purchase funds for the casino) [unverified: V1 did not find the 1836 treaty in the opinion; the majority concerns the Michigan Indian Land Claims Settlement Act, so the link is background only]
holding_summary: Tribal sovereign immunity bars Michigan's suit to enjoin an off-reservation casino; IGRA waives immunity only for gaming on Indian lands; the Court declined to overrule Kiowa.

short_name: Dollar General Corp. v. Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians
holding_summary: The Court split 4-4 (after Scalia's death), leaving in place a ruling that a tribal court could hear a tort suit against a non-member company that leased tribal land and operated a youth work program. No precedent set.

short_name: Mashpee Wampanoag trust-land litigation (Littlefield v. Dept. of the Interior line)
full_citation: Littlefield v. U.S. Dep't of the Interior, 199 F. Supp. 3d 391 (D. Mass. 2016) [from-memory]; D.D.C. 2020; D. Mass. and 1st Cir. affirmances; cert. denied Apr. 2024
court: D. Mass.; D.D.C.; 1st Cir.; U.S. Supreme Court
holding_summary: Interior's 2015 trust acquisition was remanded; in 2018 Interior said it lacked authority (Carcieri); a D.D.C. court vacated that in 2020; Interior's 2021 decision finding the Tribe under federal jurisdiction in 1934 was upheld by the district court and First Circuit, and certiorari was denied in early April 2024 [procedural history per DOJ blog].

short_name: Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin v. United States
holding_summary: Equitable tolling of a statute of limitations requires both diligence and an extraordinary circumstance beyond the litigant's control; the Tribe's contract-support-cost claims were not tolled.

The 1882 Act did not diminish the Omaha Reservation; only Congress can diminish, it must clearly say so, and settlers' expectations and demographic change cannot alone establish diminishment. Unanimous.

full_citation: 875 F.3d 896 (10th Cir. 2017) [from-memory; V1 found 875 F.3d 896 in Wikipedia (Sharp v. Murphy) only, secondary source; original panel opinion is 866 F.3d 1164]
treaty_at_issue: Creek treaties of 1832, 1833, 1856 and 1866; Curtis Act and Five Tribes Act [from-memory]
holding_summary: Held Congress never disestablished the Creek Reservation, so a Creek citizen's murder case belonged in federal court. Led to Carpenter v. Murphy / Sharp v. Murphy at the Supreme Court.

full_citation: 584 U.S. ___ (2018) (per curiam, equally divided), No. 17-269, aff'g United States v. Washington, No. 13-35474 (9th Cir. Mar. 2, 2017) (amended opinion; superseded original at 827 F.3d 836 (9th Cir. 2016); reporter cite of the amended opinion believed 853 F.3d 946 [unconfirmed])
nations: Stevens treaty tribes of western Washington (21 tribes)
holding_summary: An equally divided Court (Kennedy recused) affirmed the Ninth Circuit's holding that the treaties' fishing right includes a duty not to block salmon runs with state-owned culverts; the injunction requires replacing culverts by 2030.

full_citation: 587 U.S. ___ (2019), No. 17-532 [reporter page 587 U.S. 329 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
holding_summary: The Crow hunting right under the 1868 treaty did not expire at Wyoming statehood (Mille Lacs undercut Race Horse) and Bighorn National Forest was not categorically 'occupied' land. 5-4.

short_name: Washington State Dept. of Licensing v. Cougar Den, Inc.
full_citation: 586 U.S. ___ (2019), No. 16-1498 [reporter page 586 U.S. 347 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
holding_summary: The Yakama treaty right to travel on public highways bars Washington from applying its fuel-import tax to a Yakama enterprise hauling fuel to the reservation. Fractured 5-4 (lead opinion plus Gorsuch concurrence in the judgment).

full_citation: 591 U.S. ___ (2020), No. 18-9526 [reporter page 591 U.S. 894 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
nations: Muscogee (Creek) Nation (Mvskoke); later extended to Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Seminole [extension from-memory]
holding_summary: Land reserved for the Creek Nation remains 'Indian country' for Major Crimes Act purposes; only Congress can disestablish a reservation and no statute did so despite allotment and statehood. 5-4 (Gorsuch).
Affirmed the Tenth Circuit for the reasons in McGirt, so the Creek Reservation was not disestablished for Major Crimes Act purposes.

full_citation: 593 U.S. 345 (2021) [reporter page 345 from-memory, unconfirmed: no source V1 read prints it; No. 19-1414, date, holding verified at Justia]
holding_summary: A tribal police officer may temporarily detain and search a non-Indian on a public right-of-way within a reservation when there is a reasonable suspicion of a law violation (Montana's second exception). Unanimous (Breyer).

short_name: Yellen v. Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation
full_citation: 594 U.S. ___ (2021), No. 20-543 [reporter page 594 U.S. 338 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
nations: Alaska Native Corporations (ANCSA); Chehalis and other tribes
holding_summary: Alaska Native regional and village corporations are 'Indian tribes' under ISDEAA for CARES Act Title V funds; ANCSA eligibility satisfies the 'recognized as eligible' clause. 6-3.

full_citation: 597 U.S. ___ (2022), No. 21-429 [reporter page 597 U.S. 629 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
holding_summary: Federal and state governments have concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute non-Indians who commit crimes against Indians in Indian country. 5-4 (Kavanaugh); Gorsuch dissent.

short_name: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo v. Texas
full_citation: 596 U.S. ___ (2022), No. 20-493 [reporter page 596 U.S. 685 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
holding_summary: The Restoration Act bars gaming on the Pueblo's lands only where Texas law wholly prohibits the activity; IGRA otherwise governs. 5-4 (Gorsuch).

full_citation: 599 U.S. ___ (2023), Nos. 21-1484 and 22-51 [reporter page 599 U.S. 555 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
holding_summary: The 1868 treaty implicitly reserved water for the reservation but imposed no affirmative duty on the United States to secure water for the Nation; the Court rejected a trust-duty claim. 5-4 (Kavanaugh); Gorsuch dissent.

full_citation: 599 U.S. ___ (2023), Nos. 21-376 et al. [reporter page 599 U.S. 255 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
nations: Cherokee, Oneida, Quinault and Morongo Band (intervenor tribes) [from-memory]
holding_summary: Upheld Congress's Article I authority to enact ICWA and rejected anticommandeering challenges to its placement preferences, active-efforts and record-keeping provisions; equal protection and nondelegation claims failed for lack of standing. 7-2 (Barrett).

short_name: Lac du Flambeau Band v. Coughlin
full_citation: 599 U.S. ___ (2023), No. 22-227 [reporter page 599 U.S. 382 from-memory; matches Wikipedia infobox, secondary only; check bound volume]
nations: Lac du Flambeau Band of Lake Superior Chippewa (Anishinaabe)
holding_summary: The Bankruptcy Code unequivocally abrogates sovereign immunity for all governmental units, including tribes. Jackson wrote for the Court; Thomas concurred in the judgment and Gorsuch dissented (8-1 by the listed alignment; Justia's summary header says 7-2, so the tally is flagged).

short_name: Apache Stronghold v. United States (Oak Flat; Chi'chil Bildagoteel)
full_citation: 101 F.4th 1036 (9th Cir. 2024) (en banc), cert. denied, No. 24-291 (U.S. May 27, 2025)
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, 9th Cir. (en banc); U.S. Supreme Court
nations: Western Apache (San Carlos Apache and others; plaintiff Apache Stronghold)
treaty_at_issue: Treaty of Santa Fe (1852) invoked as trust-duty claim
holding_summary: En banc Ninth Circuit rejected RFRA and treaty-based claims to block the congressionally mandated Oak Flat land exchange to Resolution Copper [merits holding from-memory]. Supreme Court denied certiorari May 27, 2025; Gorsuch (joined by Thomas) dissented; Alito took no part [denial verified at Cornell LII].

short_name: Becerra v. San Carlos Apache Tribe
full_citation: 602 U.S. 222 (2024) (consolidated with Becerra v. Northern Arapaho Tribe)
nations: San Carlos Apache Tribe; Northern Arapaho Tribe
holding_summary: ISDEAA requires the Indian Health Service to pay contract support costs for tribes' use of third-party income (e.g., Medicare/insurance) on programs they took over. 5-4 (Roberts).

short_name: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe v. Madore (Mille Lacs County)
treaty_at_issue: Treaties of 1855, 1863 and 1864; Nelson Act of 1889
holding_summary: Dismissed as moot after Minnesota amended its law, and vacated the district court's 2022-2023 rulings that the reservation was never disestablished. The majority's Part IV said the 1863/1864 treaties and Nelson Act appear to satisfy the diminishment presumption; Judge Erickson did not join Part IV. The status question is left for a future live case.
Cert. denied, leaving in place a ruling that the Chinook recognition claim was a non-justiciable political question [lower-court ruling per NARF Tribal Supreme Court Project memo].

short_name: Lopez v. United States (Oak Flat application)
nations: Western Apache (San Carlos Apache and Apache Stronghold-affiliated plaintiffs) [from-memory]
holding_summary: The Court denied an application to stop the Oak Flat land transfer to Resolution Copper (NARF memo lists it as denied Mar. 19, 2026); the Forest Service then transferred more than 2,400 acres.

short_name: Oak Flat land-exchange litigation, Ninth Circuit (2026)
full_citation: Ninth Circuit panel decision (Mar. 2026) and denial of rehearing en banc (late Sept./early Oct. 2026); caption and F.4th cite not located
nations: Inter Tribal Association of Arizona and conservation groups as plaintiffs; Apache sacred site
holding_summary: A 2-1 panel cleared the exchange; after rehearing was denied, eleven judges urged the Supreme Court to correct what Chief Judge Murguia called a 'tragic error' (KJZZ, Oct. 2, 2026).
